passage:
For three evenings Mahima watched her cousin Sharmila leave the groundnut shelling half done and hurry toward the bank kiosk by the bus stop, phone pressed to her ear. At night Sharmila slept with the phone under her pillow and jumped whenever it buzzed.
On the fourth evening Mahima waited on the step until Sharmila came back, dusty and out of breath.
'Sit for a minute,' Mahima said, pushing the bowl toward her. 'You don't have to tell me anything. I've just noticed you running to the kiosk every day.'
Sharmila shelled two pods in silence. 'It's a prize. They need a tax first.'
Mahima didn't scold. 'Then it can wait one night. Tomorrow we'll call the bank's own number from your passbook, together. If it's real, it will still be real.'
Sharmila let out a long breath and nodded.

qa.q: Where did Sharmila hurry to each evening?
qa.a: Sharmila hurried toward the bank kiosk by the bus stop.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's long breath at the end suggest?
qa.a: It suggests relief, as if part of her had been waiting for someone to give her permission to pause.

qa.q: Which part of Mahima's approach made it easier for Sharmila to open up?
qa.a: Mahima asked without scolding, said Sharmila didn't have to explain, and suggested one night's pause and a call to the bank's own number, which felt safe rather than shaming.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling before Mahima spoke to her?
qa.a: Sharmila was probably tense and cornered, sleeping with the phone under her pillow and rushing to pay with no one to check it with.

grounding: It shows a family member noticing secrecy and hurried payments, asking gently without blame and proposing a pause to check through the bank's official number.

passage:
Sofia noticed it first on Sunday: Oskar eating toast standing up, eyes on his phone, not even hearing the kettle click off. By Wednesday he had cancelled football twice and made two bank transfers at the kitchen table, tilting the screen away from her.
On Thursday night she found him on the balcony in the cold, typing fast.
She handed him a mug of tea and leaned on the railing beside him. 'You've seemed really far away this week. I'm not angry. I just miss you.'
Oskar rubbed his face. 'There's this refund from the tax office. They say I have to pay a processing fee first. Today.'
'Okay,' Sofia said slowly. 'How about we pause till morning and ring the tax office on the number from their own website? I'll sit with you.'
He looked at the phone, then at her. 'Yeah. Okay.'

qa.q: What had Oskar cancelled twice by Wednesday?
qa.a: He had cancelled football twice.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling when she joined Oskar on the balcony?
qa.a: She was worried and missed him, but chose warmth over anger, telling him she wasn't angry and just missed him.

qa.q: What made Sofia's suggestion a good turning point?
qa.a: She proposed a short pause and a check on the number from the tax office's own website, and offered to sit with him, so he could verify without losing face.

qa.q: What might Oskar be feeling when Sofia offers to sit with him?
qa.a: He is probably relieved to share the weight, even if he is also embarrassed that his week of secrecy has been noticed.

grounding: It shows someone close noticing a person glued to the phone and making hidden transfers, then asking calmly and suggesting a pause to verify officially.

passage:
In the queue at the bank branch in Indore, Raghav watched his younger brother Abhinav fill in a transfer slip for the third time that month, a hand hiding the amount. Abhinav's phone kept buzzing; he answered in whispers, turned to the wall. For weeks he had been glued to it at dinner, and last Sunday he had asked Raghav for a loan without saying why.
Raghav's first instinct was to snatch the slip. He didn't. He waited until they sat on the plastic chairs near the fan.
"Abhinav, I'm not angry. I'm just worried about you. Who is this money going to?"
Abhinav's jaw worked. "A job agency. For Dubai. They said don't discuss it, or I'll lose the slot."
"Okay. Before you pay, can we pause ten minutes and call the official emigration helpline together? If it's real, the slot will wait."
Abhinav looked at the slip for a long moment, then folded it in half.

qa.q: What did the agency tell Abhinav not to do?
qa.a: Don't discuss it, or I'll lose the slot.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he wanted to snatch the slip?
qa.a: Raghav felt alarmed and protective, but chose calm so Abhinav wouldn't get defensive.

qa.q: Why did Raghav's approach work?
qa.a: He asked without blame and suggested a short pause to verify through an official helpline, which let Abhinav step back without losing face.

qa.q: What is Abhinav going through as he folds the slip?
qa.a: He feels torn and scared, wanting the job but beginning to doubt the agency's secrecy.

grounding: At a bank, a brother notices secrecy, rushed transfers and a phone always buzzing, asks calmly without blame and suggests pausing to verify.

passage:
Irfan,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it aloud it comes out wrong, and I don't want us to fight.
For three weeks you've been on your phone late every night, turning the screen away when I pass. Twice I've seen transfer messages from our joint account that you didn't mention. On Saturday you snapped at Inaaya for asking to play a game on your phone, and you never snap at her.
I'm not angry and I'm not blaming you. I'm worried. Whatever is going on, I'm on your side.
If someone is telling you to keep something secret or to send money quickly, can we please pause, just for one day, and check it together through the official number of whoever they claim to be? If it's genuine, a day won't hurt.
I'll make chai tonight after Inaaya sleeps. We can talk, or just sit.
Swati

qa.q: How many times has Swati seen transfer messages?
qa.a: Twice I've seen transfer messages.

qa.q: What is Swati feeling as she writes?
qa.a: Swati feels worried and loving, choosing a letter to avoid a fight and to show she isn't blaming Irfan.

qa.q: What does Swati suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: A one-day pause to check together through the official number, since scams depend on urgency and secrecy.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Irfan may feel exposed and ashamed at first, but also relieved that Swati is on his side.

grounding: A wife notices secrecy, unexplained transfers and a husband glued to his phone, and asks calmly, without blame, for a pause to verify.

passage:
Keerthana, you want to know how I found out about Papa. Little things first. He'd always been a newspaper person, and suddenly he was glued to his phone, stepping onto the balcony for calls. He stopped coming on our Sunday walks. Twice the bank's alerts about transfers he'd never mentioned arrived in the family email.
My first reaction was to confront him. I'm glad I didn't. Instead one evening I sat beside him with two cups of tea and said, "Papa, nobody's in trouble. I just see you're stressed. Who keeps calling?"
He was quiet, then showed me. A man claiming to be from a pension office, saying Papa's pension would stop unless he paid "revalidation fees" and told no one.
I said, "Let's just pause. Tomorrow we'll call the pension office on the official number from the letter they sent last year." We did. They had never heard of it. I'm Varun, and I'm still proud of Papa for showing me.

qa.q: What did the man claim Papa had to pay?
qa.a: Revalidation fees.

qa.q: How did Varun feel when the urge to confront came?
qa.a: Varun felt alarmed and frustrated, but chose calm, which later felt like the right choice.

qa.q: What made Varun's approach work?
qa.a: Sitting with tea, saying nobody was in trouble, and suggesting they check the pension office's official number together.

qa.q: What was Papa likely feeling before he showed the calls?
qa.a: Papa was probably frightened and ashamed, pressured to keep the calls secret and afraid of losing his pension.

grounding: A young adult notices a parent's secrecy, unexplained transfers and phone habit, asks calmly without blame and suggests verifying officially.

passage: I'm Gurpreet. I'll say what I saw in our flat in Shillong over those two weeks, though I can't know everything Lalremsiami felt. My wife started taking her phone into the bathroom. She'd leave dinner half eaten when it buzzed. Twice I saw her at the bank's ATM on a weekday afternoon, which she never does. When I asked, she said, "Just helping a friend." One night she was awake at two, typing fast, her face lit blue. I wanted to grab the phone. Instead I made two cups of tea and sat beside her. "You don't have to tell me everything. But whoever this is, can we call the bank together, on the number on your card, before you send anything else?" She was silent for a long time. Then she put the phone between us on the table, face up.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet see Lalremsiami twice on a weekday afternoon?
qa.a: Twice Gurpreet saw her at the bank's ATM on a weekday afternoon.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling at two in the night, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt worried and alarmed, wanting to grab the phone, but chose calm by making tea and sitting beside her.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's approach likely to work?
qa.a: Gurpreet asked calmly, without blame, did not demand the whole story and suggested one clear step: a pause to call the bank on the official number.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami be experiencing when she puts the phone face up?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and ashamed at once, finally letting someone in after two weeks of secrecy and rushed transfers.

grounding: Shows a family member noticing secrecy, rushed transfers and constant phone use, then calmly suggesting a pause to verify through an official channel.
